newsitem.title: CHINA: China bicycle makers confident despite glut.
newsitem.headline: China bicycle makers confident despite glut.

text.p: Major Chinese bicycle makers said on Friday they were confident of surviving a market glut, with the bicycle remaining the country's main form of transport.

Official figures published this week showed China's annual bicycle production capacity is 60 million to 70 million units, with actual production of 40 million and domestic demand of 30 million. Half the country's 70 major producers were in the red, the figures said.

A spokesman for Shanghai Phoenix, with domestic A share and foreign currency B shares listed in Shanghai, said the company would post a profit in 1996, with sales peaking in the second half of the year.

He put 1996 output at about 5.2 million to 5.3 million units, against an output capacity of 5.5 million. Exports in 1996 were at $60 million, up from $55 million in 1995, mainly to Latin America, East Europe, Africa and Southeast Asia.
"Our products are middle- and low-quality, and compete in different markets from the high-quality models produced by joint venture factories," he said.
A flood of joint venture factories since the mid-1980s have caused the surge in output.
One is China Giant, a Sino-Taiwan joint venture in Kunshan, a city near Shanghai.
"Supply exceeds demand in the Chinese market and some of the producers will go bankrupt," said a spokesman for China Giant. "We hope we will not be one of them."
"But overall demand is stable," he said. "In the next few years, there will be no big improvement in public transport so bicycles will remain the main form of transport."
China Giant started in 1994 with output of 750,000, exporting high- and medium-grade bicycles to the United States and Japan. It exported 150,000 to 200,000 models to Japan in 1995, he said.

A spokesman for Shanghai Forever Bicycle said that despite the market glut, it had cut inventory to 150,000 units from 230,000 at the start of the year through launching new products and expanding its sales network.
"Given economic conditions, the size of the population and road limitations in China, the bicycle will remain the primary form of transport," he said.
Shanghai Forever is increasing exports to markets that do not impose quotas on Chinese bicycles, such as in Africa, the Middle East, Eastern Europe and Southeast Asia, he said.
The company is running a profit, he said, declining to give a full 1996 estimate. In the first half, it posted a net profit of 2.3694 million yuan, down from 9.379 million in the same 1995 period.
Restrictions on Chinese models in Canada and the European Union have contributed to the glut, because bicycles originally destined for these markets have been sold domestically.
Analysts are bearish on Shanghai Forever and Phoenix.
"Forever Bicycle is stuck in a highly competitive, low-tech sunset industry with no growth prospect," one analyst at a foreign brokerage said, recommending a sell for Forever and Phoenix shares.
An analyst at a second brokerage also recommended a sell for Phoenix, citing a dull growth outlook, rising costs and insignificant earnings from outside businesses.
